instructions.4424-midterm:
Midterm Exam

The midterm is a take-home essay exam covering Modules 1–7. You will answer two of the three provided short-essay questions and one long-essay question, for a total of three responses.

Short-essay questions — answer two of the three (500 words each)

  1. Interpersonal influence vs. observational learning. Katz and Lazarsfeld's two-step flow holds that media effects reach most people indirectly, through opinion leaders who interpret and relay media content. Bandura's social cognitive theory instead emphasizes direct effects through symbolic modeling and observational learning. Drawing on both readings, explain how each account treats the role of other people in producing media effects. Then argue which account better explains how media influence operates in today's networked media environment, where audiences both consume and circulate content. Support your answer with a concrete example.
  2. Designing a persuasive campaign. A public-health agency wants to persuade young adults to get an annual flu shot. Using Petty and Cacioppo's Elaboration Likelihood Model, explain how you would design the campaign differently for (a) audience members who are highly motivated and able to think carefully about the message and (b) audience members for whom this is a low-involvement issue. Identify which route of persuasion each approach relies on, what message features or source cues you would emphasize, and why the durability of the resulting attitude change differs between routes. Draw on Valkenburg, Peter, and Walther's discussion of conditional media effects to explain why these audience differences matter.
  3. Framing vs. cultivation. Entman defines framing as selecting some aspects of a perceived reality and making them more salient so as to promote a particular problem definition, causal interpretation, moral evaluation, or treatment recommendation. Cultivation theory instead locates media effects in heavy, cumulative exposure to stable, recurring patterns across media content. Using both readings, compare how framing and cultivation each explain the formation of public beliefs about crime. Address what each theory identifies as the content responsible for the effect, the time scale on which the effect operates, and the audiences most affected.

Long-essay question — required (1,000–1,200 words)

On November 3, 2026, voters will cast ballots in the midterm elections. Choose ONE type of election-related media content — for example, local television news coverage, a national newspaper's online coverage, political advertising, or campaign content on social media — and analyze its likely effects on voters using at least three theories from Modules 1–7 (such as agenda-setting and priming, framing, cultivation theory, social cognitive theory, the elaboration likelihood model, or the two-step flow). For each theory you use: (a) state the mechanism it proposes in your own words; (b) apply that mechanism to specific features of the coverage you selected; and (c) identify one limitation of the theory for explaining this case. Conclude by arguing which single theory best explains the coverage's overall effect on voters, and why.

Write all three responses in the single editor below and label each clearly (e.g., “Short Essay — Question 2,” “Short Essay — Question 3,” “Long Essay”).

Length

  • Each short-essay response: 500 words.
  • The long-essay response: 1,000–1,200 words.
  • Word counts apply to the body of each response. In-text citations and the reference list do not count toward the limit.
  • Responses below the minimum will lose points. Exceeding the maximum by more than 10% will also lose points — edit for concision rather than padding.

Citations

  • Each essay must cite at least two assigned course readings from Modules 1–7 and engage the relevant media theories or concepts by name.
  • Use APA 7th edition in-text citations: (Author, Year) for paraphrases and (Author, Year, p. #) for direct quotations.
  • Include an APA-formatted reference list at the end of the exam covering every source you cite.
  • Outside sources are not required. If you use them, they must be scholarly or primary sources and cited the same way.

Submission

  • Type your full exam response in the editor below. Pasting into the main editor is blocked to preserve typing analytics; use the Pasted references area for citations, links, and your reference list.
  • You may submit only once. Your response is hidden from other students until after the due date.
  • The exam opens Friday, October 9 at 9:00 AM ET and is due Sunday, October 11 at 11:59 PM ET.

Academic integrity

  • Do not use generative AI tools (e.g., ChatGPT, Claude, Copilot, Gemini) for any part of this exam. All writing must be your own.
  • Do not collaborate with classmates or share exam questions or answers.
instructions.4424-final:
Final Exam

The final is a take-home essay exam covering Modules 8–14. You will answer two of the three provided short-essay questions and one long-essay question. Each short-essay response should be 300–500 words; the long-essay response should be 750–1,000 words.

Requirements

  • Cite specific readings and media theories from Modules 8–14.
  • Use APA in-text citations and include a reference list.
  • Type your full exam response in the editor below. Pasting into the main editor is blocked to preserve typing analytics; use the Pasted references area for citations, links, and references.
  • You may submit only once. Your response is hidden from other students until after the due date.
  • Do not use generative AI to draft your responses; you may use it only for grammar and spelling checks.
